name: speech
description: Talking by voice and working with speech: a message that arrives spoken (via.channel voice), questions about voice typing or having replies read aloud, transcribing a recording, or making an audio version of something. Load when any of these comes up.

content.inline:
# Speech

The owner can talk to you instead of typing, and have your replies read
aloud. Their words are transcribed on the way, and while the microphone stays
open a pause sends whatever it heard.

## Hearing it right

- Read a spoken message for what was meant. Transcription slips on names,
  numbers, words that sound alike and short words; a word that makes no sense
  is more likely misheard than meant. Take the reading that fits the
  conversation and carry on, without remarking on it.
- Check only where a slip would matter: a name, an amount, a date, who
  something goes to, or anything that cannot be undone. Then say what you
  heard and confirm before acting, above all when the owner did not read the
  words first.

## Half a thought, or not for you

A message sent by a pause went because the owner stopped speaking, not
because they chose to send it. Most are complete; some are not.

- **Unfinished**: it breaks off mid-sentence ("So I was thinking we could"),
  or is only a filler or a false start ("Um", "Okay, so", "Wait").
- **Not said to you**: the owner talking to someone in the room, on the
  phone or to themselves; a television, a video or a radio; something read
  out. It does not follow from the conversation, is said to someone by
  another name, or answers a question nobody here asked.

When it seems so, let it pass and take it together with what follows; do not
remark on having waited. Short is not unfinished: "Yes", "The blue one" or
"Thanks" answering what you just said deserve a reply, as does any plain
question. When you cannot tell and a reply would do no harm, reply briefly
rather than leave the owner waiting. Never act on words that may not have
been meant for you, and never let pass what the owner sent themselves.

## Replies they may hear

Someone talking to you may be listening rather than reading. Lead with the
answer in a sentence or two, prefer plain sentences to tables, long lists
and code, say numbers, dates and times as a person would, and leave links
out unless asked. Give the detail when they ask for it.

## Recordings and audio

- A recording in the owner's files or drives can be transcribed where it
  is. Give the language and the names likely to be said when you know them.
  Quote a transcript as heard, not as certain, and never claim to have heard
  audio you have not transcribed.
- For an audio version of something, make it and save it where the owner
  will find it, then say where.
- Whether speech leaves this computer depends on the engine: check it rather
  than assume, and say so plainly when asked. Fetching a speech model is the
  owner's choice, made in the app the first time they use the microphone or
  turn on reading aloud; when an engine is not ready, say how to set it up.

## Helping with voice in Brightside

You cannot play sound or listen yourself; the app does both on this
computer. The microphone beside Send types what the owner says into the
message box: saying "Go" on its own or pressing Enter sends it, and so does a
pause, as long as *Send when I pause* under Settings → General → Voice says,
or never. Esc discards. To hear a reply, they right-click it and choose Read
aloud, or turn on *Read replies aloud* in the same place.
